subject: Very simple negative binomial fit diverges: Stan 1.2.0

messages.author: 1718a05954397331
messages.subject: Very simple negative binomial fit diverges: Stan 1.2.0
parts:
Dear Fellow Stan Users,

Using RStan (Stan 1.2.0, R 2.15.2, Mac OS X 10.6, RStudio 0.97.318), I'm trying to fit the parameters of a simple negative binomial model. Here's the Stan code:

data {
    int N;
    int y[N];
}

parameters {
    real<lower=0> alpha;
    real<lower=0> beta;
}

model {
    // alpha ~ uniform(0,1000);
    // beta ~ uniform(0,1000);
    for (i in 1:N) {
        lp__ <- lp__ + neg_binomial_log(y[i], alpha, beta);
    }
}

and the R code calling it:

set.seed(1827) ; with(list(y=rnbinom(1000, size=10, mu=3)), model <<- stan(file="negbin_test.stan", data=list(N=length(y), y=y)))

The problem is that the estimates are reasonable for some chains, but diverge for others:

I get a bunch of the following error messages for the chains that are causing problem:

Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis rejected due to the following underlying, non-fatal (really) issue (and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Error in function stan::prob::neg_binomial_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Shape parameter is inf:0, but must be finite!
If the problem persists across multiple draws, you might have a problem with an initial state or a gradient somewhere.
 If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be drawn from the posterior.

Two observations:
  1. Uncommenting the priors in the code above reliably gives sensible estimates.  But one would hope that an informative prior should not be required in such a simple scenario, especially since the MLE is well-defined, e.g.
    > set.seed(1827) ; with(list(y=rnbinom(1000, size=10, mu=3)), model.mle <<- fitdistr(y, dnbinom, start=list(size=5, mu=1)))
    > model.mle
          size          mu    
      9.65088604   2.97100734 
     (1.85356831) (0.06233488)

  2. I find using the negative binomial rather awkward with Stan compared to JAGS. First, in JAGS, I can specify that a variable is neg-binomial using the tilde notation, e.g.
    y[t] ~ dnegbin(theta[t], n)
    whereas in Stan I need to fiddle with the lp__ accumulator (unless I misread instructions somewhere).  Moreover, the parametrization of the distribution is unlike that in either R or JAGS, which makes porting JAGS code rather inconvenient.  I may suggest adding the following equivalencies with the R parameter names to the Stan documentation:
    R: x                 Stan: n
    R: n, size           Stan: alpha
    R: p, prob           Stan: beta/(beta+1)
    R: p/(1-p)           Stan: beta
    R: mu = n(1-p)/p     Stan: beta = alpha/mu

Any guidance on these issues would be greatly appreciated!

Many thanks,
+ Nicolas Chapados

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Very simple negative binomial fit diverges: Stan 1.2.0
parts:
You need a prior on alpha and beta to keep them from
running off to infinity. Here's the sample model distributed
in src/models/basic_estimators/negative_binomial.stan:

data {
int<lower=1> N;
int<lower=0> y[N];

y[i] ~ neg_binomial(alpha, beta);
}

Those are pretty fat priors -- you should use
something reasonable for what you expect alpha and beta
to be.

And keep in mind our negative binomial has the parameterization
like the gamma-Poisson in Andrew's book Bayesian Data Analysis
(formula's in the manual).

- Bob

On Wednesday, March 13, 2013 2:13:23 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
You need a prior on alpha and beta to keep them from
running off to infinity.  Here's the sample model distributed
in src/models/basic_estimators/negative_binomial.stan:

data {
   int<lower=1> N;
   int<lower=0> y[N];
}
parameters {
   real<lower=0> alpha;
   real<lower=0> beta;
}
model {
   alpha ~ cauchy(0,10);
   beta ~ cauchy(0,10);
   for (i in 1:N)
     y[i] ~ neg_binomial(alpha, beta);
}

Those are pretty fat priors -- you should use
something reasonable for what you expect alpha and beta
to be.

And keep in mind our negative binomial has the parameterization
like the gamma-Poisson in Andrew's book Bayesian Data Analysis
(formula's in the manual).

- Bob
